title: Venn Diagrams
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that Venn diagrams with many regions, where students must generate their own examples (or argue that a region is impossible), are a versatile high-value activity, and gives ten tips for using them. The key claim is that learner-generated examples expose misconceptions that teacher-set questions miss. Most of the tips are about scaffolding the structure: start with a basic example, do a double Venn before a triple, work an example together, and supply examples to sort if students are stuck. Extensions include finding extra or most interesting examples, changing an example as little as possible to move between regions, and writing their own Venn diagram. He also addresses marking, where peer review with starred disagreements replaces projecting answers. It is a good model of how to turn a familiar task into a thinking task.
points: Generating examples is a stronger test of understanding than answering set questions, because it surfaces misconceptions the teacher did not anticipate.
Fluency with the structure comes first: begin with a simple example and a double Venn so attention can go to the content rather than the format.
Scaffold stuck students by asking them to sort given examples, which is easier than generating examples from scratch.
Extensions such as 'the most interesting example' and 'change it as little as possible' draw on boundary examples and variation theory.
Since answers are open-ended, marking must be done by swapping with a partner and discussing starred disagreements, not by projecting an answer key.
quotes: Venn Diagrams provide students with an opportunity to generate their own examples. As I discuss in my Tips for Teachers book, such learner-generated examples are a fantastic test of student understanding as they can reveal misconceptions in a way that teacher-generated questions may miss.
Students try to find examples that can fit in each of the 8 regions. If they cannot find an example to fit in a particular region, can they provide a convincing argument that it is impossible?

This helps to identify any misconceptions or misunderstandings with the Venn Diagram structure, or the subject content (rounding, in this case), which might be more difficult to unpick in the weeds of an epic triple Venn. It also makes it more likely students will taste some success, which should help motivate them to keep going at the challenge that follows.

Sorting is easier than generating one’s own examples and should help students get back into the activity. Indeed, I have seen teachers begin with 8 examples for students to sort into regions before asking them to generate their own examples.

This may appear a bit of a throwaway extension, but generating multiple examples can help students move towards generalisation. Building on this, I like to ask students who have finished to think of the most interesting example they can for a particular region, whatever they consider interesting to mean. This prompt compels students to consider boundary examples, and is a revealing insight into the strength of their understanding.

Then what is the smallest change they can make to that example so they now have an example for region B, and so on? This taps into the power of variation theory, enabling students to focus on the critical aspects of examples.

When assessing students’ work, we have the inherent problem with all learner-generated examples: there are potentially an infinite number of correct and incorrect examples for each region, so banging the answers on the board and asking students to mark them themselves will not work. Instead, ask students to swap their completed Venn Diagram with their partner.
